subject: A few things I noticed about Scotty's Auto Repair's online presence
body:
Hi Sam,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across Scotty's and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- You're ahead of most shops — full AutoRepair schema with reviews built in, and testimonials surfaced right on your own site. Strong foundation, and your reputation backs it up (Yelp ~94, Birdeye 188).

Where you're leaving money on the table
- No way to book or request a quote online. It's call-or-nothing — there isn't a single form on the site. A lot of customers, especially younger ones, won't pick up the phone; they'll fill out a form or move on to a shop that lets them.
- No after-hours capture. You're closed evenings and weekends, so anyone who finds you then has no way to lock in their spot — and they're gone by Monday.
- No live chat for the quick "can you look at my car this week?" questions that turn into booked work.

None of this is urgent, and your reputation clearly speaks for itself — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.

Best,
Leo Lebel
cheddar.lebel@gmail.com

subject: A few things I noticed about Jerl's online presence
body:
Hi Menno,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across Jerl's Muffler & Brake and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- Testimonials right on your own site, Saturday hours (better coverage than most peers), and genuinely strong reviews (Yelp 235, Birdeye 214). Solid presence.

Where you're leaving money on the table
- Your contact form doesn't look wired up — it still has a placeholder 'your@email.com' in it, which usually means submissions aren't actually going anywhere. Worth checking; a form that silently drops leads is worse than no form.
- No live chat. A lot of customers want a quick "how much for brakes on my car?" answer before they commit.
- The site is missing the behind-the-scenes Google markup (LocalBusiness/AutoRepair schema) that helps you surface for "muffler / brake shop near me" — a cheap fix that punches above its weight.

None of this is urgent, and your reputation clearly speaks for itself — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.

subject: A few things I noticed about Advanced Auto Care's online presence
body:
Hi Steve,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across Advanced Auto Care and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- Honestly, you're doing more right than most shops out here — online booking, schema with your rating and location, reviews surfaced on your own site, and NAPA + AAA approval. Strong setup.

Where you're leaving money on the table
- No live chat. You've got booking covered, but a lot of customers want to ask a quick question — "can you look at my brakes today?" — before they commit, and right now there's no way to do that on the site. Those are exactly the visitors who turn into same-week work.
- No after-hours coverage beyond the booking link. A live answer (or instant callback) for evening and weekend calls would catch the leads that don't want to wait until Monday.
- Small thing — your public contact email is a yahoo address. A branded inbox on your own domain looks more established and helps deliverability when you email customers.

You're clearly ahead of the pack, so this is fine-tuning, not fixing — but each is a little leakage worth closing.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be tightened up cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.

Best,
Leo Lebel
cheddar.lebel@gmail.com

subject: A few things I noticed about Car Services' online presence
body:
Hi Frank,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across Car Services and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- Good behind-the-scenes Google markup (LocalBusiness schema) already in place, and strong Yelp sentiment — people specifically call out your honesty and upfront pricing, which is exactly what wins repeat customers.

Where you're leaving money on the table
- Your hours aren't published anywhere on the site. Customers genuinely can't tell when you're open without calling — and many won't bother.
- Your contact form looks like an unwired template (placeholder 'user@domain.com'), which usually means submissions aren't reaching you. Worth checking — a form that silently drops leads costs you real work.
- No live chat, and after-hours it's phone-only.
- Review volume is thin (~20 on Yelp) relative to nearby shops — and since you've clearly earned the goodwill, a simple system to ask happy customers for reviews would close that gap fast.

None of this is urgent, and the shop clearly does right by people — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.
